Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.

ABSTRACT
We document five facts about payment stablecoins using wallet-level blockchain data from 2020 to 
2025. First, stablecoins serve as a transaction currency: onchain volume exceeds Bitcoin’s despite 
a much smaller supply, velocity has risen sharply, and transactions have shifted toward low-value 
transfers. Second, using transaction timing to refine exchange-based attribution, we find activity 
spread across the Americas, Europe, and Asia and fewer cross-regional flows than the standard 
method implies. Third, we estimate a structural cash-management model on the holdings data and 
find that the costs of accessing stablecoin wallets have fallen since 2023. Fourth, stablecoins are 
becoming the settlement currency of a fast-growing onchain credit market, and their growth 
appears to reallocate rather than destroy credit. Fifth, smart contracts are involved in about a third of 
Ethereum stablecoin transactions and over two thirds of volume, and protocols such as x402 
demonstrate sub-cent machine-to-machine payments. Stablecoins behave as tokenized money, with 
implications for financial markets and regulation.

1 Introduction
Stablecoins are digital currencies recorded on blockchains that maintain a stable value relative to a
unit of account, usually the U.S. dollar. Unlike Bitcoin and Ether, they are designed to serve as a
store of value and a medium of exchange on public blockchains. Because they are programmable,
they also play a key role in decentralized finance (DeFi). Based on a set of facts that we document
in this paper, we argue that stablecoins are, in effect, tokenized money.
We conduct the first comprehensive analysis of stablecoin use based on wallet-level blockchain
data, covering the period 2020 to 2025. Our analysis focuses on fiat-backed stablecoins, which
hold reserves of safe, liquid assets denominated in major fiat currencies.1 The two largest, USDT
(issuedbyTether)andUSDC(issuedbyCircle),hadacombinedmarketvalueabove$260billionin
December 2025. Fiat-backed stablecoins pay no interest and hold their value at par, so their main
use is as a means of payment. The dataset that we develop lets us classify transactions by size and
function and compare stablecoins with other payment methods on cost and turnover.

in use cases, the geography of activity, and the financial infrastructure built around stablecoins.
A second question is whether money that moves onto blockchains reduces bank deposits and the
credit they fund. We conduct a balance-sheet accounting to address this question and find little
support for the concern.

To maintain their peg, fiat-backed stablecoin issuers hold reserves that enable redemptions at
par. The composition of these reserves varies across issuers, which matters for stability and run
risk (Liao and Caramichael 2022). USDC reserves are held in two components: approximately
80 to 90 percent in short-dated U.S. Treasuries and Treasury reverse repos, managed through the
Circle Reserve Fund (an SEC-regulated government money market fund), and approximately 10
to 20 percent in cash deposits at globally systemically important banks and settlement banks.2
Liao, Hadeed, and Zeng 2023 describe this reserve structure in detail. Tether’s reserves are more
diversified: as of September 2025, approximately 77 percent is held in cash and cash equivalents
(primarilyU.S.Treasurybills),withtheremainderallocatedtopreciousmetals(7percent),secured
loans (8 percent), Bitcoin (5 percent), and other investments.3 U.S. dollar-linked stablecoins remain
dominant, although stablecoins pegged to other currencies such as euros, Mexican pesos, and
Australian dollars are also in circulation.
The stability of the peg depends on the soundness of the reserves and on the functioning of the
primary market, which is the issuance and redemption channel between the issuer and authorized
participants. In the secondary market, where stablecoins trade on exchanges, prices can deviate
from par for short periods. This happens mostly when the primary market is closed (e.g., outside
banking hours). However, deviations tend to be small and short-lived when the reserves are liquid
and the primary market works well (Liao, Hadeed, and Zeng 2023).

D.1 Tokenization as a source of credit. The credit documented in Fact 4 is created through two
channelsthatparalleltraditionalbankintermediationandpartlysubstituteforit. First,tokenization
converts otherwise illiquid assets into standardized, transferable, and programmable collateral.
Lending against imperfectly liquid collateral is the core business of banking: banks extend credit
against houses, inventories, receivables, and other assets that are costly to value and to seize.
Onchain, overcollateralized lending protocols perform the same function, with tokenized assets
pledged as collateral for stablecoin loans. Today the eligible collateral consists mostly of liquid
crypto assets. It is broadening as tokenized money market funds, Treasury securities, private
credit, andotherreal-worldassetsmoveonchain. Eachnewlytokenizedassetclasscaninprinciple
be pledged as collateral for stablecoin-denominated credit.
Second,onchaincreditprovisionismarket-basedratherthanintermediary-based. Interestrates
on lending protocols adjust algorithmically with pool utilization. Collateral haircuts and loan-to-
value limits are posted publicly. Competitive arbitrageurs liquidate undercollateralized positions
as soon as they breach their thresholds. Credit risk is thereby continuously priced, collateralized,
and marked to market. In bank-led intermediation, by contrast, much of the underlying risk is
not directly priced at the exposure level. It is held on opaque balance sheets, funded by deposits
whoseholdershavelittleabilityorincentivetomonitorit,andmanagedmainlythroughregulation
in the form of capital requirements, supervisory examination, and deposit insurance (Allen and
Gale 2000). The onchain model shifts the burden of risk management from regulatory oversight of
intermediaries toward market forces operating on transparent positions.
D.2 Rule-basedintermediationandmoralhazard. Afurtherstructuraldifferenceconcernsdis-
cretion. Traditional credit intermediation delegates substantial discretion to the intermediary in

screening borrowers, monitoring exposures, choosing risk, and timing the recognition of losses.
The agency frictions created by that delegation are a classic source of moral hazard in banking
(Diamond 1984; Holmström and Tirole 1997), particularly when the intermediary’s liabilities are
insured or implicitly guaranteed. Onchain lending protocols are designed to keep discretion to a
minimum. Collateral eligibility, loan-to-value limits, interest-rate schedules, and liquidation trig-
gers are encoded in publicly auditable smart contracts and applied uniformly to every participant.
